headlines.title: 2 men allegedly yell anti-gay slurs during on-campus beating of San Jose State student
headlines.description: Two young men face hate crime charges after they allegedly beat a San Jose State University student while yelling homophobic slurs, the Santa Clara County District Attorney’s Office announced Wednesday. Sunnyvale resident Josue Medina Flores, 19, and Fremont resident Christian Gabriel Nunez Petty, 20, were charged with felony assault with hate crime allegations in connection with the unprovoked attack on the San Jose State campus early Saturday morning, the district attorney’s office said. The male student and two female friends were walking on the campus at about 3:44 a.m. when they passed by the two suspects, according to the district attorney’s office. The suspects allegedly asked the student if he was gay and yelled anti-gay slurs at him. The student and his friends ignored the suspects and continued walking. The suspects allegedly then ran up to the student and attacked him, punching him in the head more than two dozen times and kicking him while yelling anti-gay slurs, the district attorney’s office said. The suspects allegedly also struck one of the student’s friends when she jumped on top of him to shield him from the punches and kicks. The suspects fled from the scene, but San Jose State police officers managed to arrest them before they could make it off the campus, according to district attorney’s office. The student was taken to a local hospital to be treated for his injuries and later released, the district attorney’s office said. The university’s security camera network captured video footage of the attack, the district attorney’s office said. The suspects are scheduled to be arraigned Wednesday afternoon, according to the district attorney’s office. They face prison time if they are convicted. “If you hurt someone because of their race, religion, gender, or sexuality, you will be arrested and prosecuted,” District Attorney Jeff Rosen said in a statement. “Tolerance and diversity are cherished values in this community. We back up them with one voice – and the full might of the law.”

headlines.title: Woman killed after allegedly exiting vehicle following crash on Highway 101 in San Jose
headlines.description: A 63-year-old woman was killed on Highway 101 in San Jose on Monday night after allegedly exiting her vehicle following a collision. The victim was driving northbound in a Nissan Juke when she allegedly rear-ended a Toyota Prius south of Oakland Road, according to the California Highway Patrol. The driver of the Nissan got out of her vehicle and was standing in between the two disabled vehicles on the highway when another vehicle struck the Nissan, pinning the woman between her vehicle and the Prius, according to the California Highway Patrol. The woman, who the CHP said was a San Jose resident, was pronounced dead after being taken to a hospital. The CHP said drugs and alcohol did not appear to be a factor in the 11:30 p.m. wreck. The collision remained under investigation as of Tuesday.

headlines.title: Angel Island prescribed burn to resume in Marin County
headlines.description: California State Parks, Cal Fire and the Marin County Fire Department plan to resume a prescribed burn on Angel Island State Park as early as Wednesday, two weeks after the operation was paused. Angel Island is the largest island in San Francisco Bay, about one square mile, and smoke will be visible from elsewhere around the region. Residents are asked not to call 911 to report smoke from the island. A planned burn of 260 acres that began Sept. 8 was paused after discussions with the Bay Area Air District. Smoke could be visible from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. on burn days and for up to three days afterward. The prescribed fire is intended to reduce grassland and coastal scrub fuel loads and lower the risk of a catastrophic wildfire on the island. The work is supported by Proposition 4, a bond approved by California voters in 2024 to fund climate resilience projects. So far, 62 acres have been completed. The agencies said renewed burning could continue through Thursday, depending on wildfire activity, staffing and equipment availability, weather, smoke movement and fuel moisture. “We really look for those small windows that have the greatest ability to disperse the smoke in the least impactful manner,” said Division Chief Graham Groneman with the Marin County Fire Department. Angel Island State Park will remain open during burn days. However, some trails near the burn area, including portions of the Ida Trail, Sunset Trail and the park’s fire and perimeter roads, will be closed for one to three days during and immediately after the burn. Access to the summit of Mount Livermore on the island will not be permitted on some burn days as well. Visitors are advised to follow posted closures and directions from park and fire personnel.

headlines.title: Former San Jose high school manager pleads guilty to paying minors to make porn
headlines.description: A former operations manager at a San Jose high school pleaded guilty in federal court earlier this week to two counts of online child enticement and two counts of receipt of child pornography. The charges against 46-year-old Todd Baldwin were brought by federal prosecutors after he was accused of paying underage boys — including at least one student he knew through the school where he worked, Valley Christian High School — to take pictures and film themselves engaging in sexual acts, according to the U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of California’s office. Other victims attended Live Oak High School in Morgan Hill. Baldwin was accused of paying the 16- and 17-year-old victims thousands of dollars to make pornography for his consumption and to sell online. He also collected and tried to sell their used underwear, prosecutors said. He used Snapchat, Gmail, Venmo, and CashApp to communicate with the victims and transfer money to them. Baldwin faces between a decade and life in prison. He is scheduled to be sentenced in January and remains free on bond in the meantime.

headlines.title: Local coalition calls for end to federal oversight of Oakland police
headlines.description: More than two decades after the “Oakland Riders” scandal rocked the Oakland Police Department, the city could be moving closer to running its police department without federal oversight, with a judge expected to make that decision next week. The scandal included allegations of false arrests, planted evidence and excessive force. Over the past 23 years, the Oakland Police Department has undergone 51 court-ordered reforms. On Wednesday, Safe Oakland, a coalition of neighborhood, business, civil rights and faith leaders, spoke about the reforms enacted over the past two decades and why the group believes the Oakland Police Department should be trusted to operate without federal oversight. NBC Bay Area’s Kris Sanchez has the full report in the video above. Oakland May 27 Oakland Jun 1, 2022 Oakland Police Department Enters Probation Period That Could End Federal Oversight

headlines.title: Divers search South Bay Lake for missing San Jose man Larry Nguyen
headlines.description: The search for a missing man brought Santa Clara County Sheriff’s divers to a South Bay lake Tuesday. Crews from the Santa Clara County Sheriff’s Office were seen searching Grant Lake on Mount Hamilton Road, looking for any signs of Larry Nguyen. A missing person poster has been put up near the site, noting that Nguyen was last seen on Sept. 8 when he was dropped off in a nearby parking lot. In a statement, the San Jose Police Department would only say this is an active and ongoing missing persons investigation. There is no word on whether divers found anything in the lake.

headlines.title: Ripley's Believe It or Not! to close Fisherman's Wharf location after nearly 60 years
headlines.description: After nearly six decades in operation, Ripley’s Believe It or Not! is shutting down its iconic Fisherman’s Wharf location. Jim Pattison Jr., president of Ripley’s Believe It or Not! World Entertainment, announced in a statement released Tuesday that the attraction will permanently close sometime before the end of the year.

headlines.title: Mexican Navy's ‘Cuauhtémoc' ship sails under Golden Gate Bridge ahead of 4-day visit
headlines.description: A Mexican Navy tall ship sailed into San Francisco Bay on Wednesday morning for a four-day goodwill visit, marking its first return to the city in 17 years. The ARM Cuauhtémoc BE-01 sailed beneath the Golden Gate Bridge around 8:45 a.m. before arriving at Pier 15 along The Embarcadero. The three-masted Navy training ship was greeted with fanfare as it made its official return to San Francisco. Officials from the Mexican Consulate and representatives from city government were on hand to welcome the ship, along with hundreds of crew members aboard. The visit comes after a tragic chapter in the ship’s recent history. Last year, the Cuauhtémoc struck New York’s Brooklyn Bridge, killing two people on board. The ship was commissioned in the 1980s and built in Spain. It travels to ports around the world on goodwill visits aimed at sharing Mexican culture and history. Visitors in San Francisco will have several opportunities to tour the ship during its stay. Tours are scheduled for noon to 3:30 p.m. Wednesday; 10 a.m. to noon and 4 to 8 p.m. Thursday; and 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. Friday and Saturday. The Cuauhtémoc is scheduled to depart San Francisco at 9:30 a.m. Sunday. Bay City News contributed to this report

headlines.title: Stanford University removes promotional photo altered with AI to replace student, violating policy
headlines.description: Stanford University removed a promotional photo that had been digitally altered to replace a male Hispanic student with an AI-generated Black female student without disclosure, violating university policy. The altered image breached Stanford’s policy prohibiting the use of artificial intelligence in photographs depicting people or events. Following the incident, the university removed the image and announced plans to provide additional staff training to prevent future violations.

headlines.title: Bay Area voter guide: What to know about the November 2026 election
headlines.description: What to Know — Election Day is Nov. 3, 2026 California will choose a new governor to replace Gavin Newsom, who terms out after this year. The choices are Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton. Voters will decide 14 state propositions. Regional sales tax Measure RTM, the Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, aims to increase funds for public transit. California’s Congressional District 11 race features Scott Wiener and Connie Chan competing to succeed Nancy Pelosi. Aisha Wahab and Melissa Hernandez will face off again after a special election in August where Wahab secured victory to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. All 80 California Assembly seats are up for reelection, as well as 20 Senate seats. California’s general election is Nov. 3, with statewide races and propositions as well as key local races and measures across the Bay Area. Here’s what you need to know to cast your ballot, including important dates and deadlines, how to register or check your status, where and when to vote, and what’s on the ballot. Key election dates The last day to register to vote for the Nov. 3 general election is Oct. 19. County election officials will start mailing ballots by Oct. 5. Ballot drop-off locations open on Oct. 6 Last day to register to vote for the general election is Oct. 19. First vote centers open for early in-person voting in all Voter’s Choice Act counties on Oct. 24. In person early voting locations in the state open on Oct. 31. Election Day, Nov. 3, is the last day to vote in-person or return a ballot by 8 p.m. Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Vote-by-mail ballots must be postmarked no later than Nov. 3. If mailing on election day, get a hand-stamped postmark from a postal employee inside a post office. Visit the California Secretary of State’s website for a full list of key dates and deadlines. Check voter registration status Voters can check their registration at voterstatus.sos.ca.gov to confirm their mailing address and voting status. How to register to vote California residents can register to vote in elections at registertovote.ca.gov. Note Oct. 19 is the last day to register for the general election. Same day voter registration window will be open from Oct. 20 up to the Nov. 3 election day. Visit caearlyvoting.sos.ca.gov for a list of early voting locations to complete same day registration. How to find your polling place Visit the California Secretary of State’s website, where you can input your address to find your polling location and see what is on your ballot. Voters can also visit their county elections office for more information. Scroll down to the Bay Area county election offices section of this guide for further contact information. What to bring to your polling place Voters usually are not required to show identification to a polling place worker before casting a ballot, according to the Secretary of State’s website. There are some instances when providing identification is required: Voting for the first time after registering to vote by mail and did not provide a driver license number California identification number or the last four digits of social security number are missing on registration form In these cases voters should plan to bring identification to a polling place or bring a copy of it with their vote-by-mail ballot. The Secretary of State says the following are acceptable forms of identification: Passport Driver license Official state identification card Student identification card Copy of recent utility bill Sample ballot booklet received from county elections office Any document received by a government agency How to track your mail-in ballot Voters can track their vote-by-mail ballot and confirm it has been received by using the state’s Where’s My Ballot? tool at california.ballottrax.net/voter/. Ballots mailed in may take a few days to appear on the website. Why is California choosing a new governor? Gov. Gavin Newsom terms out after this year and voters will choose between Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton, who both advanced to the general election after a wild primary. Becerra has served as former President Joe Biden’s top health official and oversaw the response to the coronavirus pandemic. He was also the California’s attorney general during President Donald Trump’s first term and has more than two decades of experience as a congressmember. Hilton was a conservative commentator with a show on Fox News for six years. He also worked as an adviser to former British prime minister David Cameron. What are the 14 California propositions voters will decide in the November election? Here’s a list of the California propositions on the November ballot and descriptions from the secretary of state: Proposition 1: Authorizes bonds for housing affordability programs Proposition 2: Increases state’s rainy day fund Proposition 3: Provides permanent funding for schools and healthcare by extending existing tax on high incomes Proposition 4: Repeals prohibition against public funding of election campaigns. Proposition 5: Changes recall election process for statewide officers. Proposition 37: Creates loan program for middle-income buyers of qualified new homes. Proposition 38: Authorizes bonds for immunology medical research. Proposition 39: Prohibits citizens from voting unless they present government-issued identification. Proposition 40: Imposes one-time tax on certain taxpayers. Proposition 41: Prohibits new state taxes that exclude revenues from state spending limit. Requires audits for new state special taxes. Proposition 42: Prohibits new state personal property taxes and certain retroactive state taxes. Proposition 43: Limits voters’ ability to raise revenues for local government services. Proposition 44: Requires community health clinics spend 90% of revenue on program services. Proposition 45: Modifies environmental review for certain projects. Regional measure to watch Measure RTM: The Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, is a regional sales tax aimed at increasing funds for public transit. It includes 5 Bay Area counties: Alameda, Contra Costa, San Francisco, San Mateo, and Santa Clara. Races and measures to watch in Alameda County California Congressional District 14: California lawmaker Aisha Wahab and Bay Area Rapid Transit Director Melissa Hernandez will face off again to determine who will serve the next full two-year term. Wahab topped Hernandez in an August special election to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. Swalwell resigned from Congress earlier this year after sexual assault and misconduct allegations. District 14 includes the East Bay cities such as Fremont, Hayward and Livermore. Measure X in Berkeley: Would establish 10% limit on annual rent increases and other changes to the city’s rent ordinance. Measure Y in Berkeley: Parcel tax to pay for arts projects. Measure Z in Berkeley: Parcel tax to fund a public bank. Measure AA in Berkeley: Increase soda tax (not assigned) Measure EE in Oakland: Shift city to a strong mayor system. Measure FF in Oakland: Eliminate foreclosure exemption from property transfer tax. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Alameda County and additional election information, visit the Alameda County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Contra Costa County In Contra Costa County, several county board of education seats are open. In Richmond, residents will vote on a new mayor while voters in San Pablo will weigh in on Measure S, which would limit rent increases. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Contra Costa County and additional election information, visit the Contra Costa County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Napa County California Congressional District 4: Mike Thompson faces Eric Jones. Measure B in Napa County: Sales tax to fund wildfire prevention and open space preservation. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Napa County and additional election information, visit the Napa County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in San Francisco San Francisco voters will weigh in on several open seats on the county board of supervisors and board of education. Proposition A: Give mayor more power to hire and fire department heads. Proposition B: Pave way for public bank. Proposition C: Increase the city’s annual contribution to an affordable housing trust fund. Proposition D: New barriers to placing measures on the ballot. Proposition E: Changes to city contracting. Proposition G: Reopen parts of the Great Highway to vehicle traffic on weekdays. Proposition H: Parcel tax to fund Muni. Proposition J: Eliminate foreclosure exemption from property transfer tax California Congressional District 11: Scott Wiener and Connie Chan compete to succeed Nancy Pelosi. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in San Francisco and additional election information, visit the San Francisco Department of Elections website. Races and measures to watch in San Mateo County Measure E in Redwood City: Limit rent increases. Measure Q in Half Moon Bay: Referendum to block proposed farmworker housing. Measure U in San Mateo County: Create independent commission to draw supervisor districts. For a complete list of San Mateo County measures and races on the ballot, visit smacre.gov/elections. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in San Mateo County and additional election information, visit the San Mateo County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Santa Clara County In San Jose, incumbents Peter Ortiz and Bien Doan are up for re-election in Districts 5 and 7, respectively, and there’s an open seat in District 9. Races and measures to watch in Solano County Solano County Board of Supervisors, District 4: Mike Silva and John Carli face in a runoff in a district covering Vacaville and Dixon. Measure E in Solano County: New tax on data centers and battery storage facilities in the unincorporated county areas. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Solano County and additional election information, visit the Solano County Registrar of Voters website. Races and measures to watch in Sonoma County California Congressional District 1: Mike McGuire will face James Gallagher in a seat redistricted by Proposition 50. California Congressional District 4: Mike Thompson faces Eric Jones. State Assembly District 12: Eric Lucan and Jackie Elward compete in a battle between business and labor. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Sonoma County and additional election information, visit the Sonoma County Registrar of Voters website. headlines.title: San Francisco Fleet Week 2026: Events, schedules, what to know
headlines.description: It’s that time of year again. San Francisco Fleet Week is back. The fall tradition will be highlighted by the Blue Angels screaming across the skies, but there are plenty of other events to experience. Check out the guide below to learn more about Fleet Week events. What is San Francisco Fleet Week? San Francisco Fleet Week is an annual celebration of the nation’s sea services. A multi-day air show, parade of ships and ship tours highlight the weeklong festivities. “San Francisco Fleet Week is an annual public event that honors the contributions of the men and women of the United States Armed Forces while advancing cooperation and knowledge among civilian- and military-based Humanitarian Assistance personnel,” a statement on the event’s website reads. When is San Francisco Fleet Week 2026? Fleet Week is scheduled to take place Sunday, Oct. 4 through Monday, Oct. 12. headlines.title: San Jose considers new rules for license plate reader cameras
headlines.description: San Jose city leaders are moving toward setting new rules for the use of license plate reader cameras after the city’s police chief acknowledged that an officer used data from the system for personal use. Wednesday marks the first step toward creating rules governing the cameras, which San Jose Police Chief Paul Joseph has said are serious crime-fighting tools. Among the rules that could be enacted are prohibiting access from non-police devices, strengthening audits and pursuing state legislation regarding unauthorized access. Some community members and organizations have been pushing the city to get rid of the Flock cameras or rein in their use. The issue came to a head after it was uncovered that a San Jose police officer used license plate reader data to help a family member. “I was furious. I was furious that an officer would betray the public trust in that manner, that he would not understand how serious of a violation this is,” Joseph said. SIREN community organizer Kimberly Woo raised broader concerns about the cameras. “Mass surveillance is not public safety, and these cameras are only creating new threats,” Woo said. “Again, it goes way beyond just one officer and one vendor and one company because overwhelming evidence has shown, across the country, local agencies and ALPR vendors have grossly mishandled and abused our data.” The issue will go before the city’s Rules Committee. Its recommendation will then go to the San Jose City Council.
